newsitem.title: FRANCE: NATO lawmakers back Belarus over "crazy" president.
newsitem.headline: NATO lawmakers back Belarus over "crazy" president.

text.p: Western parliaments gave vocal backing to the Belarus Supreme Soviet (parliament) on Monday in its tug-of-war with President Alexander Lukashenko, accused of seeking to turn the former Soviet republic into a dictatorship.

The North Atlantic Assembly, grouping parliamentarians from 40 European and North American countries including the 16 NATO states, voiced strong support for the Belarus parliament in its bid to prevent Lukashenko changing the constitution to introduce presidential rule.
Assembly president Karsten Voigt of Germany told a news conference that Lukashenko's behaviour was "illegal, non-democratic and sometimes even crazy".

"We as the North Atlantic Assembly...are in favour of strong parliamentary rule in Belarus. Insofar as the president of Belarus is endangering this parliamentary power, influence and stability, we act in solidarity with our colleagues in Belarus, who need support from outside," he said.
Voigt said it was the duty of all democratic legislatures, including Russia's Duma, to support democracy and the rule of law in Belarus.

Lukashenko has called a referendum for November 24 to amend the constitution and tighten his grip on rival institutions after firing the head of the independent election commission and ignoring rulings by the constitutional court.
Voigt provided a platform, at the start of the Assembly's annual session in Paris, for the head of the Belarus delegation, Mecheslau Gryb, to denounce Lukashenko.

Gryb, a former head of the Belarus Supreme Soviet, charged that the president was trying to rig next Sunday's vote by manipulating absentee ballots, muzzling the media, barring opposition campaign finance and using the security forces to intimidate parliament and protesters.
"I would like to stress that there is a real threat from the repeated efforts of the president and his team to take power and establish a dictatorship," he said.

Since Lukashenko's critics were barred from state radio and television, the only way they could get a message across to voters was via Russia's three television networks, which can be seen in parts of Belarus.

In the latest challenge to the authoritarian president on Monday, previously loyal Prime Minister Mikhail Chigir was quoted by parliamentary leaders in Minsk as saying he would resign unless Lukashenko cancelled the referendum.
Voigt also warned that Lukashenko would be in violation of international agreements if Belarus did not hand over its 18 remaining nuclear missiles to Russia by the end of this year.

With six weeks to go, no preparations have been made for the weapons to be transferred and Lukashenko has hinted he may keep them because of the "threat" from NATO plans to expand by admitting several former communist Central European states.
